Disability accommodation means adjusting a club's physical space, materials, or session pace so a student with a physical, sensory, or learning disability can participate as fully as any other student -- a ramp and an accessible restroom for a student using a wheelchair, large-print or high-contrast challenge cards for a student with low vision, noise-reducing headphones or a quieter corner for a student with sensory sensitivity, or simply more time on a task for a student who processes instructions more slowly. Accommodation is specific to the student in front of a mentor, not a single checklist that treats every disability the same way.

A worked example: a student who is hard of hearing joins a club that runs sessions in a large, echoing room where a mentor's spoken instructions are difficult to follow over background noise from other groups. Rather than assuming the student will simply keep up or fall behind, the mentor asks the student directly what would help, and the answer is straightforward: written instructions on an index card alongside the spoken version, and a seat near the front rather than in the back corner. Both changes cost nothing and take five minutes to set up each session. The mentor also checks the venue's accessible entrance and confirms it stays unlocked during club hours, since a technically compliant ramp that's chained shut during the exact hours a club meets accommodates no one.

You don't need to be a disability-law expert to accommodate one student well

If the range of possible accommodations feels overwhelming, that's normal -- most mentors aren't trained in accessibility law, and they don't need to be. Start with one direct question to the student or family in front of you ("what would make this easier?"), and build the fix from their answer instead of trying to anticipate every possible need in advance.

docs.title: Diagram: Access Barrier to Fix Map
docs.text:
Access Barrier to Fix Map

Type: graph-model sim-id: access-barrier-to-fix-map Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Purpose: Let a mentor see, in one view, how each structural barrier covered in this chapter connects to the concrete club practice that addresses it, and notice where a single fix resolves more than one barrier at once.

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine

Learning objective: Given a barrier a family might face (cost, transportation, inflexible timing, language, or disability access), the learner examines which club practice from this chapter addresses it, and identifies practices that address more than one barrier.

Node types: 1. Barrier nodes (5, red circles, left column) -- Cost, Transportation, Inflexible Timing, Language, Disability Access 2. Fix nodes (6, green squares, right column) -- No-Fee Model, Scholarship Fund, Free Device Loan Program, Carpool/Transit/Virtual Option, Alternating Saturday + Weekday Sessions, Translated Materials + Bilingual Contact, Direct Accommodation Request

Edges (ADDRESSED_BY, directional arrows from barrier to fix): - Cost -> No-Fee Model - Cost -> Scholarship Fund - Cost -> Free Device Loan Program - Transportation -> Carpool/Transit/Virtual Option - Inflexible Timing -> Alternating Saturday + Weekday Sessions - Language -> Translated Materials + Bilingual Contact - Disability Access -> Direct Accommodation Request

Sample data note: Cost has three outgoing edges, the only barrier with more than one fix converging on it -- the pattern the diagram is built to surface, since a single policy decision like going no-fee doesn't fully solve cost alone; it takes a scholarship fund and a device loan program alongside it.

Layout: Hierarchical left-to-right, barriers in the left column, fixes in the right column

Interactive features: - Hover a barrier node: show a one-line plain-language description of the barrier - Click a barrier node: highlight all connected fix nodes and dim the rest; open a side-panel infobox with the barrier's definition and its worked-example scenario from this chapter - Click a fix node: highlight all barriers it addresses, making it visible that the no-fee model alone only reaches one edge of the cost problem - Zoom: mouse wheel; Pan: click-and-drag background

Visual styling: red circles for barriers, green squares for fixes, constant arrow thickness, label text directly on each node

Legend: barrier color/shape versus fix color/shape, plus a note that arrow direction always reads "barrier is addressed by fix"

Implementation: vis-network JavaScript library rendering a small fixed dataset (5 barrier nodes, 6 fix nodes, 7 edges) defined in a data.json file; canvas width is responsive, height fixed to match the iframe.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Reaching a genuinely representative club roster starts with recruiting minorities and recruiting girls and women through channels that travel beyond a mentor's existing network, backed by underserved community outreach that names a specific under-reached population rather than treating diversity as one generic goal, and made real through language accessibility and carefully checked translated materials. None of that outreach holds up if cost quietly filters families back out: low income family support, a genuine no-fee club model, and an honest accounting of why no fees matters all depend on the scholarship fund and free device loan program that fund the promise rather than just declare it -- work that Chapter 30's budgeting and grant-writing content makes possible. Even a free, well-promoted club can still lose students to a transportation barrier, an inflexible session time, or a disability accommodation nobody thought to ask about, which is why each of those barriers is treated here as a solvable logistics problem, not a reason a student didn't show up.

You just built a club that widens its own door instead of waiting by it

You just connected recruiting, funding, and logistics into one picture: a club that reaches underserved families, backs its no-fee promise with real funding, and removes the transportation, timing, and accessibility barriers that quietly decide who gets to stay. That's the structural work behind a roster that actually reflects your community.

docs.title: Quiz: Reaching Underserved Communities and Removing Barriers
docs.text: Test your understanding of recruiting a genuinely diverse club roster and removing the cost, language, transportation, timing, and disability barriers that keep families away with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is underserved community outreach?
docs.text:
1. A single flyer posted in the library lobby
  2. A scholarship application requiring a family to state financial need
  3. A checklist of accessibility features for a building's entrance
  4. The broader practice of identifying which populations near a club are least likely to hear about it and building a deliberate plan to reach them, naming that population specifically rather than pursuing outreach in the abstract
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter defines underserved community outreach as identifying a specific under-reached population, such as families relying on a resettlement agency, and building a deliberate plan to reach them, rather than pursuing generic outreach. Option A describes a single limited channel, exactly the kind of narrow approach the chapter warns against. Option B confuses this with an unrelated scholarship process. Option C confuses outreach with disability accommodation, a separate concept.

Concept Tested: Underserved Community Outreach See: Underserved Community Outreach

docs.title: 2. What is a scholarship fund?
docs.text:
1. A club-owned laptop lent to a student for the semester
  2. A pool of money a club sets aside to cover costs a no-fee model doesn't fully eliminate, such as a specialized kit or transportation, without singling out which family needed the help
  3. A written translation of a permission slip
  4. A carpool arrangement between two families
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter defines a scholarship fund as money set aside to cover costs a no-fee model doesn't absorb, such as an advanced elective's sensor kit, accessed through a single checkbox so a request looks identical to not needing one. Option A describes a free device loan program, a related but distinct support. Option C describes translated materials, an unrelated language-access tool. Option D describes a transportation barrier solution, a different kind of support entirely.

Concept Tested: Scholarship Fund See: Scholarship Fund

docs.title: 3. What is disability accommodation, as the chapter defines it?
docs.text:
1. Adjusting a club's physical space, materials, or session pace so a student with a physical, sensory, or learning disability can participate as fully as any other student, specific to the student in front of a mentor rather than a single checklist
  2. A single universal checklist applied identically to every student regardless of need
  3. A fee waiver granted only to students who submit medical documentation
  4. A rule limiting disability accommodations to students on the advanced track
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter's worked example shows a mentor asking a hard-of-hearing student directly what would help, then providing written instructions and a front-row seat -- accommodation specific to that student, not a generic checklist. Option B directly contradicts the chapter's explicit point that accommodation isn't a single checklist treating every disability the same. Option C invents a documentation requirement the chapter never mentions. Option D fabricates a track restriction not discussed anywhere in the chapter.

Concept Tested: Disability Accommodation See: Disability Accommodation

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter say announcing a no-fee policy on the very first flyer, before identifying a funding source, is risky?
docs.text:
1. Because a no-fee club is illegal without a state permit
  2. Because a no-fee policy automatically disqualifies a club from every grant
  3. Because costs can outpace a leader's personal contributions, tempting a mid-semester fee that betrays the families who joined specifically because the club was free
  4. Because families never notice whether a club charges a fee or not
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's worked example shows exactly this risk: laptop-repair and supply costs outpace personal funding by month three, and adding a mid-semester fee causes families who joined for the free promise to feel misled and drop out. Option A invents a legal permit requirement the chapter never discusses. Option B fabricates a grant-disqualification claim with no support in the text. Option D contradicts the chapter's entire argument about how strongly a fee signals exclusion.

Concept Tested: No Fee Club Model See: No Fee Club Model

docs.title: 5. Why does the chapter insist that a translated document be checked by a fluent speaker rather than relying on a single machine-translation pass?
docs.text:
1. Because machine translation is always more expensive than a human translator
  2. Because automated tools frequently mangle idioms, technical terms, and culturally specific phrasing, and an uncaught error can flip a document's actual meaning
  3. Because machine translation tools cannot produce a printable document
  4. Because fluent-speaker review is legally required for any document sent home with a student
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's worked example shows a machine-translated permission slip flipping "no fee required" into something closer to "fee not guaranteed," causing families to skip returning the slip until a fluent speaker caught the error. Option A makes an unsupported cost comparison the chapter never discusses. Option C invents a technical limitation of translation tools that has nothing to do with the actual concern. Option D fabricates a legal requirement not stated in the chapter.

Concept Tested: Translated Materials See: Translated Materials

docs.title: 6. According to the chapter's "why no fees matters" reasoning, what does a modest fee like $15 or $20 do beyond simply excluding families who can't pay it?
docs.text:
1. It has no effect beyond the dollar amount itself
  2. It automatically increases a club's liability insurance costs
  3. It signals to some families who could technically afford it that the club isn't really meant for them, implying equipment, prior experience, or selectivity that isn't actually true
  4. It guarantees higher-quality mentoring than a free club can offer
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's worked comparison of two nearly identical clubs shows the fee-based one drawing far fewer families, since surveyed families assumed the fee implied equipment, experience, or selection requirements that were never actually true. Option A directly contradicts the chapter's central argument about what a fee silently communicates. Option B invents an insurance-cost connection the chapter never makes. Option D fabricates a quality claim the chapter explicitly says is untrue, since both clubs offered identical curriculum and ratio.

Concept Tested: Why No Fees Matters See: Why No Fees Matters

docs.title: 7. A club sets up its scholarship fund so that a single checkbox on the standard sign-up form ("kits are available at no cost, just check this box") grants access, rather than requiring a separate financial-need application. Why does the chapter say this design matters?
docs.text:
1. It reduces the club's total spending on kits
  2. It allows the club to track exactly which families are low-income for grant reporting
  3. It is required by the club's data privacy policy
  4. A separate application or a public request adds a shame cost that keeps families from using a fund they genuinely qualify for, while a checkbox on the standard form looks identical to not needing one
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter's warning is explicit: making a family ask for help in front of other parents or fill out a separate need-based form adds a shame cost that keeps eligible families from using the fund, which is why the checkbox is built into the standard form everyone sees. Option A misstates the purpose, which is about access dignity, not reducing spending. Option B directly contradicts the chapter's point that the request should look identical to not needing one, not create an identifiable list. Option C invents a data-privacy connection the chapter never makes.

Concept Tested: Scholarship Fund See: Scholarship Fund

docs.title: 8. A club charges no registration fee but asks each family to bring a $15 supply kit for the first project. Two students stop attending right after that request, and a follow-up call reveals both families couldn't spare the $15. What does the chapter say this illustrates?
docs.text:
1. A cost doesn't have to be labeled "registration" to function as one -- any required out-of-pocket expense can silently exclude the same families a no-fee policy was meant to include, which is why low income family support means auditing every cost a family might encounter
  2. The two students simply lost interest in the club and would have left regardless
  3. The club should immediately charge a full registration fee instead of a supply kit request
  4. Supply kits are always cheaper when purchased individually by each family
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter's own worked example describes exactly this scenario and draws exactly this conclusion, generalizing that low income family support requires auditing every cost, not only the headline registration price. Option B contradicts the chapter's explicit finding that cost, not disinterest, caused the drop-off. Option C proposes the opposite of the chapter's actual fix, which was moving the cost into the club's own bulk-purchased budget. Option D reverses the chapter's point, which favors bulk purchasing by the club over individual family purchases.

Concept Tested: Low Income Family Support See: Low Income Family Support

docs.title: 9. A student who attended enthusiastically for a month suddenly stops coming. A phone call reveals the parent's work schedule changed and they can no longer drive the 20-minute route to the club. The mentor connects the family with another club parent who lives nearby and already drives past the venue. Which concept does this illustrate?
docs.text:
1. Accessible session timing
  2. Disability accommodation
  3. Recruiting girls and women
  4. A transportation barrier solution, treating a missed session as a solvable logistics problem such as an informal carpool rather than a sign of lost interest
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter's own worked example describes exactly this carpool fix, requiring no club budget or new policy, just a mentor treating a transportation gap as solvable logistics. Option A describes adjusting meeting days and times, a different barrier from a driving-distance problem. Option B describes physical or sensory accommodations, unrelated to a transportation gap. Option C describes an unrelated recruiting-equity concept, not a logistics fix for an existing student.

Concept Tested: Transportation Barrier Solution See: Transportation Barrier Solution

docs.title: 10. In the chapter's access barrier map, the "Cost" barrier has three outgoing fix connections -- the no-fee model, the scholarship fund, and the free device loan program -- while every other barrier connects to only one fix. What does this pattern suggest about addressing cost as a barrier?
docs.text:
1. Cost is not actually a real barrier for most families
  2. The other four barriers in the chapter do not require any club action at all
  3. A single policy decision like going no-fee doesn't fully solve the cost barrier alone; it takes a scholarship fund and a device loan program alongside it to cover costs the base no-fee policy doesn't eliminate
  4. Transportation and language barriers are more important to address than cost
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's own diagram note explains that cost's three converging fixes are deliberate: a no-fee policy alone doesn't fully solve cost, since a scholarship fund and device loan program are still needed to cover costs the base policy doesn't absorb, such as a specialized kit or a missing laptop. Option A contradicts the chapter's extensive treatment of cost as a major, well-documented barrier. Option B misreads the diagram, since every barrier node connects to at least one active fix requiring club action. Option D makes an unsupported priority ranking the chapter's diagram does not establish.

Concept Tested: Scholarship Fund See: Scholarship Fund

docs.title: Building Trust and Representation in Your Club
Building Trust and Representation in Your Club
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers building trust with communities a club has not yet reached, through culturally responsive teaching, curriculum representation, and partnerships with faith-based, rural, urban, and immigrant-serving organizations. It closes with a practical equity audit you can run on your own club. You will be able to run an equity audit and identify one new community partnership to pursue.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 13 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept CIS Score Assistive Technology Option 13 Culturally Responsive Teaching 12 Representation In Curriculum 11 Female Mentor Recruitment 10 Role Model Visibility 9 Community Trust Building 8 Faith Based Venue Partnership 7 Rural Community Outreach 6 Urban Community Outreach 5 Immigrant Family Outreach 4 Equity Audit Of Club 3 Inclusive Marketing Materials 2 Bias Awareness Training 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • 28. Reaching Underserved Communities and Removing Barriers

Chapter 28 removed the structural barriers that keep families from walking in the door -- cost, distance, timing, and language. Removing a barrier only gets a family to the doorway. It does not, by itself, convince anyone that the room on the other side was built with them in mind. A student who never sees anyone who looks like them leading a session, whose curriculum only ever names one kind of person as a computing pioneer, or whose family has never been personally invited by someone their own community already trusts, can walk through a wide-open, fee-free door and still quietly decide the club isn't really for them. This chapter is about that second, quieter barrier: trust and representation, and the concrete actions -- who a club puts in front of students as a mentor, what its curriculum shows, which local organizations it partners with as equals, and how it checks its own blind spots -- that close it.

This chapter is about who a student sees when they look around the room

Let's build something great -- and "great" has to include the student who hasn't pictured themselves in it yet. This chapter walks through who your club recruits as a visible mentor, what your curriculum shows, which communities you partner with as equals, and how an honest equity audit turns all three into a concrete to-do list.

docs.title: Seeing Yourself in the Club: Curriculum and Mentors
Culturally Responsive Teaching
docs.text:
Culturally responsive teaching means connecting a lesson's examples, project themes, and challenge-card framing to the cultural backgrounds and everyday experiences already present in the room, instead of defaulting to a single cultural frame and quietly treating it as neutral. It is about how a topic gets taught and illustrated -- the metaphors a mentor reaches for, the sample project themes offered, the names used in code examples -- not about who gets credited in the printed material, which is a related but separate concept covered next.

A worked example: a club's standard challenge cards all frame projects around American football statistics and Halloween costume themes, which land easily with some students and blankly with others -- a recent immigrant who has never watched a football game, or a student whose family doesn't celebrate Halloween, has to first translate the example before they can even start on the coding concept underneath it. A mentor rewrites one challenge-card set so students choose from three project themes instead of one -- a sports-stats tracker, a favorite-recipe organizer, and a music-playlist sorter -- and lets students substitute their own data. The programming concept, a sorting algorithm, never changes; only the on-ramp into it does. Attendance on challenge nights becomes more even across the group, because no student has to clear a cultural hurdle before reaching the technical one.

docs.title: Representation In Curriculum
docs.text:
Representation in curriculum is about whose faces, names, and stories actually appear inside a club's own material -- the computing pioneers highlighted in a slide, the sample photos on a challenge card, the "did you know" facts a mentor shares between projects. It is distinct from culturally responsive teaching: a lesson can be taught with perfectly relevant, locally grounded examples and still only ever credit one narrow slice of people as the ones who built the field.

A worked example: a club's standard slide deck on "computing history" names only two people -- both well-known male tech founders -- across an entire semester. A mentor adds a short, five-minute "pioneer of the week" segment tied to whatever topic is already on the schedule: Katherine Johnson when the group covers coordinate systems for turtle graphics, Radia Perlman when a lesson touches networking basics, Jerry Lawson when the group builds anything with LEDs. No new class time is added -- the segment replaces a few minutes of the existing warm-up -- but by the end of the semester the roster of people credited with building computing looks nothing like the narrow slide deck it replaced.

A club's curriculum is probably narrower than it should be if:

  • Every named computing pioneer in a semester's material is the same gender or race.
  • Every sample project photo shows the same kind of student doing the same kind of activity.
  • No lesson has ever referenced a contribution from outside the United States.
  • A mentor can't name, without looking it up, a single woman or person of color credited anywhere in the club's own slides or cards.

docs.title: Female Mentor Recruitment
docs.text:
Female mentor recruitment is the deliberate effort to bring women into a club's mentor team specifically, as distinct from recruiting girls as students, which Chapter 28 already covered. A club can succeed completely at recruiting girl students and still send the unintended message that computing is something girls learn but men lead, if every adult running a session is male. Recruiting a female mentor addresses that gap directly: it puts a woman in the room in a professional, near-peer role, not only a participant role.

A worked example: a club leader posts a mentor call in a general engineering alumni group and gets eight replies, all men. Rather than accepting that as the available pool, the leader also reaches out directly to a university's women-in-engineering alumni chapter and asks the club's one existing female mentor to personally invite two colleagues she knows from her own workplace -- a personal invitation from someone already in the role reliably outperforms a generic posting. Two women join the mentor team the following month, both citing the personal outreach, not the general call, as the reason they applied.

docs.title: Role Model Visibility
docs.text:
Role model visibility is the aggregate, lived effect of representation and mentor recruitment combined: whether students actually see an adult who shares their background leading, demonstrating, and being asked hard questions in front of the group -- not just whether that adult is technically on the roster. A club can recruit a female mentor and still fail at role model visibility if she is consistently assigned to check-in and supply management while male mentors run every visible project demonstration.

A worked example: a club's one female mentor has run the sign-in table for an entire semester while two male mentors rotate through leading the "front of room" project walkthroughs each week. A visiting parent later mentions that her daughter assumed the sign-in mentor "wasn't really a coder" because she never saw her at the whiteboard. The club leader restructures the weekly rotation so every mentor, including the check-in mentor, leads at least one front-of-room demonstration per month. Within a few sessions, three girls start lingering after the demonstration specifically to ask that mentor follow-up questions -- questions they had never directed at the male mentors leading the same kind of demo.

Presence isn't the same as visibility

Notice the shift here: a mentor who exists on your roster hasn't necessarily been seen leading anything. A student pictures themselves in a role by watching someone like them actually do it in front of the room -- not by knowing, abstractly, that such a person is somewhere in the building.

docs.title: Earning Trust Through Community Partnership
docs.text: Representation changes what a student sees once they're already in the room. Reaching families who haven't yet walked in at all is a different, earlier problem -- one that depends less on curriculum and more on whether a community already trusts the person doing the inviting.

docs.title: Community Trust Building
docs.text:
Community trust building is the practice of earning a community's confidence through consistent, low-pressure presence and follow-through, rather than through a single well-worded outreach message. Trust accumulates the way a savings account does: a leader who shows up, listens, and delivers on small promises repeatedly earns more standing than one who arrives once with a polished pitch and a request attached.

A worked example: one club leader emails a community center's director cold, asking in the first message for free meeting space and help recruiting students. The director never responds. A second leader, in a different town, attends the same kind of community center's open community meeting three times over two months without asking for anything, simply introducing the club and answering questions when asked. By the fourth visit, the center's director offers the space unprompted, because the leader had already demonstrated -- through repeated, low-stakes presence -- that the club was a real, reliable commitment rather than a one-time favor request.

Listen twice before you ask once

Here's a shortcut that saves months of cold outreach: visit a community organization's own regular meeting or event at least twice, asking nothing, before you ever request a room, a referral, or a flyer posting. Trust built by listening first outlasts trust attempted by asking first.

docs.title: Faith Based Venue Partnership
docs.text:
A faith-based venue partnership means meeting in space offered by a church, mosque, synagogue, temple, or other congregation -- spaces that often come with free or low-cost rooms and an already-engaged family network, since congregations regularly run youth and family programming of their own. The partnership works best when a club approaches the congregation's education or youth-program coordinator, not necessarily clergy directly, and when the club is explicit that its own programming stays secular regardless of which building hosts it.

A worked example: a club partners with a mosque's community center, which offers free meeting space two evenings a week and direct access to a youth program that already reaches dozens of local families. The mentor works with the center's youth coordinator rather than approaching the imam directly, schedules sessions around prayer times the coordinator identifies, and keeps all club content and challenge cards religiously neutral. The flyer for the club explicitly notes the venue is open to all families regardless of faith, which the coordinator specifically requested so the partnership would read as a shared community resource rather than a recruitment tool for the congregation.

A shared building isn't a shared belief system

Watch out for this trap: assuming that meeting in a congregation's space means club content should reflect that congregation's beliefs, or that only families of that faith are welcome. Keep the club's own programming secular, and say plainly on every flyer that the venue is open to any family in the community -- the partnership should widen the door, never narrow it.

docs.title: Rural Community Outreach
docs.text:
Rural community outreach addresses the specific mix of challenges and existing strengths in a rural area: long driving distances between families, fewer standalone STEM organizations to partner with, but often stronger, longstanding community hubs than a dense city offers -- a county extension office, a grange hall, a 4-H chapter, or the single local library branch that most families in the county already use. The fix isn't to treat rural families as simply harder to reach; it's to identify which hub already has their trust and plug into it.

A worked example: a club forming in a farming county struggles to get sign-ups through the usual school-newsletter channel, since several families homeschool or attend schools outside the county entirely. The mentor instead contacts the county's 4-H extension office, which already sends a printed newsletter to nearly every farm family in the county and runs an annual county fair most families attend in person. The club's flyer runs in that newsletter, and the mentor sets up a table at the fair rather than relying only on digital sign-ups. The mentor also shifts the club's schedule to avoid the two weeks of fall harvest, when most rural families are unavailable regardless of how good the outreach is. Sign-ups more than double compared to the school-newsletter-only approach.

docs.title: Urban Community Outreach
docs.text: Urban community outreach recognizes that a dense city doesn't mean one citywide audience -- it means many distinct neighborhoods, each with its own trusted local hub: a specific recreation center, a specific library branch, a specific block's community board. A single citywide flyer or press release usually reaches almost no one, because urban families trust the hub closest to them, not "the city" in the abstract. A club serving one neighborhood should identify that neighborhood's own recreation center or library branch and build a relationship with the staff there, the same way a rural club builds one with a county extension office.

docs.title: Immigrant Family Outreach
docs.text:
Immigrant family outreach goes beyond the translated materials and language accessibility covered in Chapter 28 -- it means building an ongoing relationship with the specific organizations an immigrant community already relies on, such as a resettlement agency, an ESL program, or a cultural or hometown association, and understanding that some families expect a personal introduction from someone they already trust rather than a flyer alone. A caseworker or association leader who vouches for a club in person, even briefly, often does more than any printed material translated into a family's home language.

Here is how the three outreach contexts above compare on where trust already sits and what a club needs to plan around:

Community Context Primary Trusted Hub Constraint to Plan Around Rural County extension office, grange hall, 4-H chapter, or the single local library branch Long driving distances; harvest-season scheduling conflicts Urban One specific neighborhood's recreation center or library branch -- never a citywide channel Many distinct neighborhoods, each with its own hub; no single message reaches all of them Immigrant-Serving Resettlement agency, ESL program, or cultural/hometown association Families often expect a personal introduction from a trusted messenger, not a flyer alone

docs.title: Making the Club Physically and Technically Accessible
docs.text: Trust and representation open the door; a club still has to make sure every student who walks through it can physically use what's inside. Chapter 28's disability accommodation covered the room itself -- ramps, seating, and pace. The next concept covers the tools students use once they're at the table.

docs.title: Assistive Technology Option
docs.text:
An assistive technology option is a specific tool, device, or software feature that lets a student with a physical, sensory, or learning difference use the same club activities as everyone else -- distinct from Chapter 28's disability accommodation, which covered the physical room and pace. Assistive technology is about the equipment and software layer: screen readers and text-to-speech for a student with a reading disability, switch-access or oversized-button input devices for a student with limited fine motor control, screen magnification for low vision, and captioned video for a student who is deaf or hard of hearing.

A worked example: a student with limited fine-motor control struggles to double-click precisely enough to run Scratch projects using the club's standard trackpads. Rather than assuming the student will simply adapt, the mentor swaps in a single large-button switch adapter connected through a USB hub, configured so one big press does what a double-click normally does. The mentor also enables a free text-to-speech browser extension for a different student who reads challenge cards more slowly than the group's pace, so that student can have any card read aloud on request instead of falling behind while everyone else moves on. Neither fix costs more than the price of one inexpensive adapter, and both let a student use the exact same project as their peers rather than a simplified substitute.

A club's assistive technology kit doesn't need to anticipate every possible need in advance -- a short list covers most common requests:

  • A switch-access or oversized-button input device for students with limited fine motor control.
  • A free text-to-speech browser extension or app for reading challenge cards aloud.
  • Screen magnification, built into every major operating system at no extra cost.
  • Closed captions turned on by default for any video content the club shows.

docs.title: Running Your Own Equity Audit
docs.text: Every concept in this chapter -- curriculum, mentors, partnerships, and assistive technology -- can drift quietly out of alignment over a year of normal club operation, one small decision at a time, without anyone noticing until a student or parent points it out. An equity audit is how a leader catches that drift on a schedule instead of by accident.

docs.title: Equity Audit Of Club
docs.text: An equity audit of a club is a structured, periodic self-review that checks a club's actual practices -- not its intentions -- against specific criteria covering curriculum representation, mentor team makeup, community partnership reach, accessibility, and marketing materials, producing a short, prioritized list of what to fix next. Run it on a fixed schedule, such as once per semester, rather than only when a problem is already visible.

docs.title: Diagram: Coding Club Equity Audit Checklist
docs.text:
Coding Club Equity Audit Checklist

Type: microsim sim-id: equity-audit-checklist Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Give a club leader a genuinely usable, run-it-today checklist that scores the club's current practices across the five areas covered in this chapter and names the single lowest-scoring area to fix first.

Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate (L5) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: assess

Learning objective: Given the club's own current practices, the learner scores each of five equity-audit categories on a simple present/partial/absent scale and identifies the lowest-scoring category as the next priority.

Canvas layout: - Top (60px): Title bar and "Reset Audit" button - Left (65%): Five category panels, each expandable, each containing 2-3 checklist items - Right (35%): Running score by category (bar per category, 0-100%) and a "Lowest Scoring Category" callout box

Categories and checklist items (each item is a 3-state toggle: Absent = 0, Partial = 1, Present = 2):

  1. Curriculum Representation
  2. "Named pioneers in our material include more than one gender and one race."

  3. "Sample project photos and themes reflect more than one cultural background."

  4. Mentor Team

  5. "At least one mentor from an underrepresented group leads visible, front-of-room demonstrations, not only support tasks."

  6. "Our mentor recruiting reaches beyond one existing personal network."

  7. Community Partnership

  8. "We have an active partnership with at least one faith-based, rural-hub, urban-neighborhood, or immigrant-serving organization."

  9. "That partnership involved us showing up and listening before we asked for anything."

  10. Accessibility

  11. "We have at least one assistive technology option on hand (switch access, text-to-speech, magnification, captions)."

  12. "A student or family has been asked directly what accommodation would help them, in the last term."

  13. Marketing Materials

  14. "Our flyers and sign-up materials show diverse, non-stereotyped imagery."
  15. "Our promotional language has been checked by someone outside the existing mentor team."

Interactive controls: - Click any checklist item to cycle it through Absent / Partial / Present - Category panels expand/collapse on click - "Reset Audit" button clears all items back to Absent - Automatic "Lowest Scoring Category" callout updates live as items change, naming the category and suggesting the single lowest-scoring item within it as the next concrete action

Behavior: each category's bar fills proportionally to its items' total score out of the category maximum, color-coded red (0-33%), yellow (34-66%), green (67-100%); the callout box always names exactly one category and one item, never a generic "keep improving" message, so the leader leaves with one concrete next step rather than a vague score.

Instructional rationale: This matches the Evaluate-level checklist pattern because the chapter's own closing outcome asks the reader to run an equity audit and identify one concrete next action; a scored, item-level checklist -- rather than a single overall club rating -- produces exactly that one prioritized action instead of an abstract sense of "doing fine" or "needs work."

Implementation: p5.js for the panel layout, toggle states, and color-coded bars; the fifteen checklist items and category structure are stored in a small JavaScript data array, since the fixed item set doesn't need an external data.json file.

Running this checklist once tells a leader exactly where the club stands today; running it on a fixed schedule is what keeps a gap from quietly reopening a year later.

Run the audit on a calendar, not a crisis

Here's a shortcut: put the equity audit on the same recurring calendar reminder as your event retrospective from earlier in this book, once a semester, so it happens on a schedule instead of only after a parent raises a concern. Fixing the single lowest-scoring item each term beats trying to fix everything at once.

docs.title: Inclusive Marketing Materials
docs.text: Inclusive marketing materials are a club's flyers, web pages, and sign-up forms designed and checked against the same representation criteria the promotional-materials rubric in Chapter 28 applied to recruiting girls, women, and minority students -- diverse imagery, plain language about cost, and language accessibility -- extended here to also reflect the community partnerships and role-model visibility this chapter covers. A marketing piece is inclusive when someone outside the existing mentor team, ideally from a community the club wants to reach, reviews it before it goes out, not only when it looks diverse to the person who made it.

docs.title: Bias Awareness Training
docs.text:
Bias awareness training helps mentors notice their own unconscious assumptions about who "looks like" a good coder, so that attention, encouragement, and opportunities to lead don't quietly flow toward students who happen to resemble a mentor's own background. It doesn't require a formal course: a short discussion of real scenarios -- who gets called on first, whose mistakes get framed as "still learning" versus "not a good fit" -- at a regular mentor meeting accomplishes the same goal.

Noticing your own bias is uncomfortable, and that discomfort is normal

If sitting with your own possible blind spots feels uncomfortable, that discomfort is a normal, expected part of the process -- not a sign you're doing something wrong. Start small: pick one recent session and ask which students you called on first, then build the conversation from what you notice.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
A club that reaches a genuinely representative roster still has to convince every student in the room that it was built with them in mind -- through culturally responsive teaching and curriculum representation that shows more than one kind of person building computing, and through female mentor recruitment and role model visibility that make sure representation is actually seen leading, not just present on a roster. None of that matters to a family the club hasn't reached yet, which is why community trust building, faith-based venue partnerships, and outreach shaped to a specific rural, urban, or immigrant community's own trusted messengers matter just as much as anything printed on a flyer. Assistive technology options make sure every student who does arrive can use the same activities as everyone else, and a scheduled equity audit -- backed by inclusive marketing materials and honest bias awareness training -- is how a leader catches the next gap before a family has to point it out.

You just built a club that earns trust instead of assuming it

You just connected representation, community partnership, and accessibility into one practical toolkit -- capped off with an equity audit you can run this semester. That's the difference between a club that's technically open to everyone and one that's actually earned the trust of everyone it hopes to reach.

docs.title: Quiz: Building Trust and Representation in Your Club
docs.text: Test your understanding of earning trust with communities a club has not yet reached, curriculum representation, visible role models, and community partnerships with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. How does culturally responsive teaching differ from representation in curriculum?
docs.text:
1. They are the same concept described with two different names
  2. Culturally responsive teaching is about how a topic gets taught and illustrated, using relevant metaphors and project themes, while representation in curriculum is about whose faces, names, and stories actually appear in the club's material
  3. Representation in curriculum only applies to challenge cards, never to slide decks
  4. Culturally responsive teaching requires translated materials, while representation in curriculum does not
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter explicitly distinguishes the two: culturally responsive teaching is about the metaphors and project themes used to teach a concept, while representation in curriculum is about who gets credited and shown in the club's own material -- a lesson can do one well and still fail the other. Option A ignores this explicit distinction the chapter draws. Option C invents a challenge-card-only restriction not stated in the chapter. Option D confuses representation with translated materials, a separate Chapter 28 concept.

Concept Tested: Culturally Responsive Teaching See: Culturally Responsive Teaching

docs.title: 2. What is role model visibility?
docs.text:
1. The number of women who have applied to be a mentor
  2. A written policy stating a club welcomes all genders
  3. A translated version of a club's promotional flyer
  4. The aggregate, lived effect of representation and mentor recruitment combined -- whether students actually see an adult who shares their background leading and demonstrating in front of the group, not just being technically on the roster
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter's worked example shows a female mentor who ran the sign-in table all semester, technically present but never seen leading -- role model visibility means being seen actually doing the work, not just being listed as a mentor. Option A describes recruitment numbers, not the visibility effect itself. Option B describes an abstract policy statement, not lived visibility. Option C describes translated materials, an unrelated language-access concept.

Concept Tested: Role Model Visibility See: Role Model Visibility

docs.title: 3. How does an assistive technology option differ from Chapter 28's disability accommodation?
docs.text:
1. Assistive technology options are only available to advanced-track students
  2. They are the same concept, and Chapter 28 simply used a different name for it
  3. An assistive technology option is a specific tool, device, or software feature -- such as a switch-access adapter or text-to-speech -- while disability accommodation covers the physical room and pace
  4. Disability accommodation is always more expensive than an assistive technology option
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter explicitly distinguishes the two: assistive technology is the equipment and software layer, like a switch-access adapter or text-to-speech extension, while disability accommodation from Chapter 28 covers the physical room, ramps, seating, and pace. Option A invents a track restriction not discussed anywhere in the chapter. Option B ignores the chapter's explicit distinction between the two concepts. Option D makes an unsupported cost comparison the chapter never states.

Concept Tested: Assistive Technology Option See: Assistive Technology Option

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter recommend a leader visit a community organization's regular meeting at least twice, asking for nothing, before requesting a room or a referral?
docs.text:
1. Because trust accumulates through consistent, low-pressure presence and follow-through, and a leader who shows up repeatedly without an immediate ask earns more standing than one who arrives once with a polished pitch and a request attached
  2. Because most community organizations require a formal written application before any request
  3. Because a single visit is against most venues' insurance policies
  4. Because community organizations only meet twice per year
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter's own worked comparison shows a cold email going unanswered while a leader who attended three meetings without asking for anything received an unprompted space offer by the fourth visit, illustrating that trust builds through repeated low-stakes presence. Option B invents a formal-application requirement the chapter never mentions. Option C fabricates an insurance restriction unrelated to community trust building. Option D makes an unsupported and implausible claim about meeting frequency.

Concept Tested: Community Trust Building See: Community Trust Building

docs.title: 5. Why does the chapter say a single citywide flyer usually reaches almost no one in urban community outreach?
docs.text:
1. Because citywide flyers cost more to print than neighborhood-specific ones
  2. Because cities do not have any community centers or library branches
  3. Because urban outreach is illegal without a city permit
  4. Because a dense city is actually many distinct neighborhoods, each with its own trusted local hub, and urban families trust the hub closest to them rather than "the city" in the abstract
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter explains that a dense city is actually many distinct neighborhoods, each with its own trusted local hub -- a specific recreation center or library branch -- so urban families trust the hub closest to them rather than a generic citywide message. Option A makes an unsupported cost claim unrelated to the actual reasoning given. Option B is factually wrong, since the chapter explicitly names recreation centers and library branches as urban outreach hubs. Option C invents a permit requirement not discussed in the chapter.

Concept Tested: Urban Community Outreach See: Urban Community Outreach

docs.title: 6. How does female mentor recruitment differ from recruiting girls and women, the Chapter 28 concept it builds on?
docs.text:
1. They are identical concepts, just used in different chapters
  2. Female mentor recruitment brings women into the club's mentor team specifically, as adults in a professional role, while recruiting girls and women (Chapter 28) targets students joining as participants
  3. Female mentor recruitment only applies to clubs with more than twenty students
  4. Recruiting girls and women requires a signed data sharing agreement, while female mentor recruitment does not
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter explicitly distinguishes female mentor recruitment as bringing women into the mentor team specifically, distinct from recruiting girls as students, since a club can succeed at the latter while still sending an unintended message if every adult running a session is male. Option A ignores the chapter's explicit distinction between the two concepts. Option C invents a club-size restriction the chapter never states. Option D fabricates a data-sharing-agreement requirement unrelated to either recruiting concept.

Concept Tested: Female Mentor Recruitment See: Female Mentor Recruitment

docs.title: 7. A club partners with a mosque's community center for free meeting space. The mentor works with the youth coordinator rather than the imam directly, schedules around prayer times, keeps all content secular, and notes on the flyer that the venue is open to all families regardless of faith. What does this illustrate?
docs.text:
1. Bias awareness training
  2. Inclusive marketing materials
  3. A faith-based venue partnership, which works best when a club approaches the education or youth-program coordinator and keeps its own programming secular regardless of which building hosts it
  4. Role model visibility
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's own worked example describes exactly this partnership, emphasizing working with the youth coordinator, scheduling around prayer times, staying secular, and stating openly that the venue welcomes any family. Option A describes mentor self-reflection training, unrelated to a venue partnership. Option B describes flyer and sign-up form design more broadly, not specifically this partnership arrangement. Option D describes visible leadership by underrepresented mentors, unrelated to venue arrangements.

Concept Tested: Faith Based Venue Partnership See: Faith Based Venue Partnership

docs.title: 8. A club forming in a farming county struggles with sign-ups through the school newsletter, since many families homeschool or attend schools outside the county. The mentor instead partners with the county's 4-H extension office and sets up a table at the county fair, and sign-ups more than double. Which concept does this illustrate?
docs.text:
1. Assistive technology option
  2. Urban community outreach
  3. Immigrant family outreach
  4. Rural community outreach, which identifies which existing community hub already has a rural family's trust -- such as a county extension office or 4-H chapter -- rather than treating rural families as simply harder to reach
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter's own worked example describes exactly this scenario, showing rural outreach succeeding by plugging into an already-trusted hub like the 4-H extension office rather than relying solely on a school-based channel. Option A describes equipment for students with disabilities, unrelated to outreach channels. Option B describes a fundamentally different context of many distinct city neighborhoods, not a farming county. Option C describes outreach to immigrant-serving organizations, unrelated to this rural scenario.

Concept Tested: Rural Community Outreach See: Rural Community Outreach

docs.title: 9. At a regular mentor meeting, the group discusses real scenarios -- who gets called on first, whose mistakes get framed as "still learning" versus "not a good fit" -- to help mentors notice their own unconscious assumptions about who "looks like" a good coder. Which concept does this describe?
docs.text:
1. Equity audit of club
  2. Bias awareness training, which helps mentors notice their own unconscious assumptions so attention and opportunities to lead don't quietly flow toward students who resemble a mentor's own background
  3. Community trust building
  4. Inclusive marketing materials
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter describes bias awareness training as exactly this kind of scenario-based discussion at a mentor meeting, requiring no formal course, aimed at noticing unconscious assumptions about who "looks like" a good coder. Option A describes a structured, scored review of club practices, a different and more formal process. Option C describes earning an outside community's confidence, unrelated to internal mentor reflection. Option D describes flyer and form design, unrelated to a mentor discussion.

Concept Tested: Bias Awareness Training See: Bias Awareness Training

docs.title: 10. The chapter's equity audit checklist always names exactly one lowest-scoring category and one specific item within it, rather than displaying a generic "keep improving" message. Why does the chapter design the audit this way?
docs.text:
1. Because a scored, item-level checklist naming one concrete next action gives a leader something specific to fix, rather than leaving them with only an abstract sense of "doing fine" or "needs work"
  2. Because a generic message would violate the club's data privacy policy
  3. Because naming only one category is a technical limitation of the audit tool that could not be fixed
  4. Because every club scores identically on all five categories, so only one needs to be shown
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter's instructional rationale is explicit: naming one concrete next action produces a prioritized to-do item instead of a vague overall impression, matching the chapter's outcome of identifying one concrete next step to pursue. Option B invents a data-privacy connection that has nothing to do with audit design. Option C mischaracterizes a deliberate design choice as an unavoidable technical limitation. Option D makes an unsupported and implausible claim that every club scores identically.

Concept Tested: Equity Audit Of Club See: Equity Audit Of Club

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers building a club budget from recurring and one-time costs, then raising the funds to support it: grant writing, corporate sponsorship, crowdfunding, and community support drives. You will be able to draft a basic club budget and a short grant proposal.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 18 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept CIS Score Establishing A Budget 254 Budget Line Item 48 Recurring Cost Planning 47 One Time Cost Planning 46 Cost Per Student Estimate 45 Raising Funds 44 Grant Writing Basics 43 Grant Proposal Structure 29 Grant Application Tracking 28 Community Support Drive 27 Crowdfunding Campaign 26 Corporate Sponsorship 25 In Kind Donation 24 Fundraising Event Planning 23 Local Company Partnership 22 Strategic Partnership Building 21 Vendor Discount Negotiation 20 Nonprofit Fiscal Sponsorship 19

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • 3. Writing Your Club Charter and Safety Policies

Chapter 3's charter already named who has authority over spending -- a decision-making process that reserves high-stakes financial calls for a mentor vote or, where one exists, an oversight board. That process only means something once there is an actual budget to vote on. Chapter 28 went a step further and explained why a coding club that charges no fee reaches a wider slice of its community than one that charges even a modest fee, but it stopped short of explaining how a leader actually pays for that promise. This chapter closes that gap: building a realistic first-year budget, understanding why recurring costs and one-time costs behave differently, and then raising the money -- through grants, community drives, corporate sponsors, and negotiated partnerships -- that lets a no-fee club stay no-fee past its first semester.

Every dollar in this chapter traces back to a real club decision

Let's build something great -- and every great club eventually needs a budget that survives contact with real invoices, not just a hopeful number scrawled on a grant application. This chapter walks through building that budget, then raising the funds through grants, sponsorships, community drives, and negotiated partnerships that keep it funded past opening day.

docs.title: Establishing A Budget
docs.text:
Establishing a budget means building a complete, written plan for every dollar a club expects to spend in a coming year, organized so a leader can see at a glance what has to be paid for again and again versus what gets paid for once and is then finished. A budget is not the same thing as a wish list of things a club would like to own -- it is a commitment to a specific total, broken into specific line items, that someone has to actually raise or already has in hand.

Think of a club budget the way you would think of a recipe. Every time you cook the same dish, certain ingredients get used up and have to be restocked -- flour, eggs, cooking oil -- no matter how many times you have made the dish before. Other purchases happen once and then sit in the kitchen for years: the oven, the mixing bowl, the good chef's knife. A club budget works the same way. Recurring costs are the flour and eggs of a coding club -- internet access, insurance, a fresh supply of printed challenge cards -- consumed every term and needing to be bought again. One-time costs are the oven and the mixer -- laptops, project kits, a storage cart -- purchased once and then reused, term after term, without buying the whole batch over again.

Here is that same distinction laid out side by side, since a leader will return to it every time a new expense shows up:

Aspect Recurring Cost One-Time Cost Repeats how often Every session, month, or year Once, or on a multi-year replacement cycle Example Internet plan, liability insurance, printed cards Laptops, project kits, a storage cart Budgeting risk if ignored Quietly drains a budget that looked fully funded Feels affordable in isolation, then arrives all at once Who usually funds it Ongoing grants, membership drives, sponsors Startup grants, in-kind donations, one-time gifts

A worked example turns this into real arithmetic. A new club forming at a public library plans to serve twelve students. Its recurring costs for the year total a \(20-per-month internet hotspot plan (\)240), a $350 annual liability insurance policy, $180 in replenished snacks and consumable supplies, and $60 in printing -- $830 in recurring costs. Its one-time costs cover six Chromebooks at \(250 apiece (\)1,500), ten Moving Rainbow kits at \(15 each (\)150), three starter robot kits at \(20 each (\)60), and a $120 storage cart -- $1,830 in one-time costs. The first year's total budget is $830 plus $1,830, or $2,660, which works out to about $221.67 per student. In year two, none of the one-time costs repeat, so the budget drops to the $830 recurring total alone -- about $69.17 per student -- a number worth remembering when a funder asks whether a grant is a one-time favor or an ongoing commitment.

The MicroSim below lets you build a budget like this one yourself, swapping in your own line items and watching the recurring split, the one-time split, and the resulting cost per student update as you go.

docs.title: Diagram: Coding Club Budget Builder
docs.text:
Coding Club Budget Builder

Type: microsim sim-id: coding-club-budget-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/economics-course/tree/main/docs/sims/budget-builder

Purpose: Let a club leader build a full first-year budget out of individual line items, then see the recurring/one-time split and the resulting cost per student before committing to a real number.

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: calculate

Learning objective: Given a set of named recurring and one-time cost line items and a student count, the learner calculates the total annual budget, the recurring-versus-one-time split, and the cost per student.

Instructional Rationale: A parameter-exploration pattern fits this Apply-level objective because the learner needs to add, remove, and reclassify several line items and immediately see the arithmetic consequences, rather than watch one pre-computed scenario play out.

Canvas layout: - Left (60%): a stacked bar showing the recurring total and one-time total side by side, plus a large "Cost Per Student" readout - Right (40%): a scrollable list of line items with add/remove controls, and the number-of-students input

Interactive controls: - Button row: "Add Recurring Item" and "Add One-Time Item," each opening a name field and a dollar-amount field - Per-item: a small "x" remove button - Input (number): Number of students, default 12 - Button: "Load Sample Year-1 Budget" -- prefills the exact worked example above (internet, insurance, snacks, printing as recurring; Chromebooks, Moving Rainbow kits, robot kits, storage cart as one-time) - Button: "Reset"

Behavior: - Recurring Total = sum of all items marked recurring - One-Time Total = sum of all items marked one-time - Total Budget = Recurring Total + One-Time Total - Cost Per Student = Total Budget / Number of Students, rounded to the nearest cent - The stacked bar and the Cost Per Student readout recalculate immediately whenever any item, amount, or the student count changes

Default parameters: loads with the sample Year-1 budget from the worked example (12 students, $830 recurring, $1,830 one-time, $2,660 total, $221.67 per student)

Implementation notes: p5.js canvas with createButton and createInput controls parented to the sketch's own control div; store line items in a JavaScript array of {name, amount, type} objects so items can be added and removed without redrawing the whole layout from scratch.

Notice which half of the recipe you're looking at

Notice the shift here: a one-time cost isn't really "done" forever -- a laptop bought once still wears out on a multi-year cycle, which means today's one-time purchase is tomorrow's recurring replacement line. Budgeting well means planning for both timelines at once, not just the one due this month.

docs.title: Breaking the Budget into Line Items
Budget Line Item
docs.text:
A budget line item is a single named entry in a budget, carrying its own dollar amount, so a leader can examine, adjust, or seek funding for one specific cost without treating the whole budget as an indivisible lump sum. "Supplies" is not a usable line item on its own; "cardstock for challenge cards, $22" is, because it names exactly what the money buys and lets a leader cut, keep, or fund that one item independently of everything else.

A worked example shows the difference in practice. A first-time club leader drafts a budget with a single line: "Materials -- \(400." When a local business offers to sponsor "whatever the club needs most," the leader has nothing specific to hand them. After breaking that one line into itemized entries -- tape and glue (\)25), cardstock (\(22), a replacement soldering iron tip (\)8), USB cables ($35), and a $310 laptop repair reserve -- the same conversation goes differently: the sponsor picks the laptop repair reserve specifically, because it is the one item large enough and concrete enough to feel like a meaningful gift. Line items turn a vague number into something a funder can actually choose to fund.

docs.title: Recurring Cost Planning
docs.text:
Recurring cost planning is the practice of identifying every cost that repeats on a predictable schedule -- every session, every month, or every year -- and budgeting for it continuously rather than treating it as a single expense that gets paid and forgotten. A cost that seems small in any single month can add up to a serious annual commitment once it repeats often enough.

A worked example makes the compounding visible. A club's $20-per-month internet hotspot plan looks trivial next to a $1,500 laptop purchase, but over a three-year planning horizon it totals $720 -- nearly half the cost of the entire laptop fleet. A leader who only plans one term ahead might not notice that this "small" recurring line is on track to outspend a much larger one-time purchase within a few years, which is exactly why recurring cost planning is treated as its own skill rather than folded into the one-time budget as an afterthought.

docs.title: One Time Cost Planning
docs.text:
One-time cost planning covers costs incurred once, typically at a club's startup or when it adds a new capability, that do not need to be repeated every year -- though, as the earlier metaphor noted, even a one-time cost eventually recurs on a longer replacement cycle. Planning for it well means distinguishing a true single purchase from a cost that only feels one-time because nobody has hit the replacement point yet.

A worked example shows why that distinction matters. A club buys six Chromebooks for $1,500 and books the entire amount as a one-time cost for the year. Three years later, two of the six devices fail and need replacing at $250 each -- a $500 expense the original one-time budget never accounted for. A more accurate plan treats the laptop purchase as "one-time" in the year it happens, but also sets aside a small annual reserve -- roughly $375 a year, spreading the $1,500 across a four-year expected lifespan -- so the eventual replacement never arrives as a surprise.

docs.title: Cost Per Student Estimate
docs.text:
A cost per student estimate divides a club's total budget, recurring and one-time costs combined, by the number of students it serves, producing a single number that is easy to compare across terms or explain to a funder who asks what it actually costs to serve one student. It is the number that turns an abstract budget total into something a grant reviewer or a sponsor can weigh against their own priorities.

Returning to the worked example from earlier in this chapter: the first year's $2,660 total budget, divided across 12 students, comes to $221.67 per student. The second year's $830 recurring-only budget, divided across the same 12 students, comes to about $69.17 per student. A leader pitching a renewal grant can use that second, much smaller number to make a direct case: the expensive part of funding this club already happened, and an ongoing grant now buys three times the reach per dollar that the startup grant did.

docs.title: Raising Funds
docs.text:
Raising funds is the general practice of securing money and in-kind resources from outside a club's own pockets to cover its budget -- an umbrella term for the specific channels the rest of this chapter details, since no single technique reliably covers an entire club budget on its own. Most sustainable clubs run several funding channels at once rather than betting everything on one.

A worked example shows what that mix looks like in practice. To cover its $2,660 first-year budget, a club leader combines a $1,600 startup microgrant (60% of the total), a $665 corporate sponsorship from a local business (25%), and $395 raised through a community support drive at a school open house (15%). No single source had to cover the whole amount, which also meant no single funder's rejection would have sunk the club's first year.

docs.title: Grant Writing Basics
docs.text:
Grant writing basics cover what a grant actually is -- money awarded by a foundation, government agency, or company based on a written application that the funder evaluates against its own stated priorities -- and the core discipline of matching a club's request to those priorities in the funder's own language, rather than describing the club in whatever terms feel natural to the person writing the application.

A worked example shows the payoff of that discipline. A local library foundation's grant guidelines state a priority for "youth STEM programming that serves underrepresented students." A first draft of a club's application describes "a fun coding club for kids," which never mentions STEM or underrepresented students at all, even though the club's own no-fee model and outreach plan from Chapter 28 already fit that priority closely. Rewriting the same facts using the funder's own language -- "youth STEM programming reaching students who face cost and access barriers to computing education" -- describes the identical club, but now speaks directly to what the reviewer was told to look for.

Your first grant application is not supposed to feel easy

If staring at a blank grant application feels intimidating, that is completely normal -- most first-time club leaders feel exactly the same way. Start by copying the funder's own priority language into your draft first, then fill in your club's real facts underneath it; the blank page gets much shorter once you're not inventing the structure from scratch.

docs.title: Grant Proposal Structure
docs.text:
Grant proposal structure is the set of standard sections nearly every grant application shares, regardless of funder: a needs statement, a project description, a budget, an evaluation plan, and a short organizational background. Learning this structure once means a leader can reuse most of a proposal's content across many different applications, adjusting only the language and numbers each funder specifically asks for.

Here is how the $500 library-foundation microgrant from the earlier example fills each section:

Section What It Covers This Club's Content Needs Statement Why the problem matters, backed by a fact or figure Local families report no free after-school STEM option within walking distance Project Description What the club will actually do Weekly no-fee coding club serving 12 students, ages 10-14, using Scratch and physical computing Budget Line items the grant will cover $500 toward the $1,830 one-time device and kit costs Evaluation Plan How success will be measured Attendance tracking and a post-session survey, from Chapter 1's continuous-improvement log Organizational Background Who is running it and why they're credible Club leader's experience, fiscal sponsor's nonprofit status (see below)

docs.title: Grant Application Tracking
docs.text:
Grant application tracking is the practice of recording every grant a club applies for -- the funder's name, amount requested, deadline, current status, and next follow-up date -- in one place, so that a promising application never quietly falls through the cracks between a founder's other responsibilities. A club applying to more than two or three funders at once needs this discipline, since memory alone stops being reliable past that point.

A worked example shows the cost of skipping it. One club leader keeps grant deadlines only in email, and misses a required progress report for a grant already awarded -- a report the funder needed thirty days before considering a renewal. The grant is not renewed the following year, and the leader only discovers why months later. A second club leader keeps a single spreadsheet with columns for funder, amount, deadline, status, and next action, and sets a calendar reminder two weeks before every deadline. That leader's renewal report goes in on time, and the funder renews the grant at a higher amount the following cycle.

One spreadsheet beats a folder full of good intentions

Here's a shortcut: keep one spreadsheet with a row per grant -- funder, amount, deadline, status, and next action -- and set a calendar reminder two weeks before every deadline, including report deadlines on grants you've already won. A missed renewal report is the single most common way a club loses funding it already had.

The workflow below traces a grant from the moment a leader spots an opportunity through the tracking step that keeps it from being forgotten.

docs.title: Diagram: Grant Writing and Tracking Workflow
docs.text:
Grant Writing and Tracking Workflow

Type: workflow sim-id: grant-writing-tracking-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Purpose: Show the full sequence from spotting a grant opportunity through writing, submitting, and tracking it to a final outcome, so a first-time grant writer knows exactly what step comes next.

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: implement

Learning objective: Given a grant opportunity at any stage, the learner correctly identifies the next step in the club's grant-writing and tracking process.

Steps (flowchart with a decision diamond): 1. Start: "Grant Opportunity Identified" -- click reveals "A foundation, company, or government program with funding priorities that plausibly match the club's mission." 2. Process: "Match Club Facts to Funder's Language" -- click reveals "Rewrite the club's real activities using the funder's own stated priority terms, per Grant Writing Basics." 3. Process: "Draft Using Standard Proposal Structure" -- click reveals "Needs statement, project description, budget, evaluation plan, organizational background." 4. Process: "Submit Before Deadline" -- click reveals "Log the submission immediately in the tracking spreadsheet with status 'Submitted.'" 5.
